sources.record: Martín Enríquez, Viceroy of New Spain, letter to Felipe II, Mexico, 5 December 1573. Blair & Robertson (eds.), *The Philippine Islands, 1493–1898*, vol. 3 (Cleveland, 1903), pp. 209–219. Translated by Francis W. Snow from *Cartas de Indias* (Madrid, 1877).
sources.perspective: The Spanish viceroy writing to the king. He wants the Philippine venture supplied and paid for, and he doubts the China trade. Chinese statements reach him second-hand.

position.proximity: Contemporary; writing from Mexico, with news brought by the ships
position.interests: Supplying the Philippine venture while doubting the China trade

sources.record: "Las nuevas que escriven de las yslas del Poniente", Hernando Riquel and others, sent from Mexico, 11 January 1574. B&R vol. 3, pp. 230–249 (read pp. 243–248). Spanish and English printed side by side; translated by Jose M. Asensio from a manuscript at Simancas.
sources.form: Primary document, a relation made from letters written at Manila in 1573
sources.perspective: Spanish officials at Manila. The cargo list at its end "was apparently added by the officials in Mexico" (B&R footnote, p. 247). The best 1573 witness for the Chinese side of the Manila trade that I could read.

position.proximity: Contemporary; letters written at Manila in 1573
position.role: Spanish officials and a government notary at Manila
position.note: SB01 and SB02 report the same ships; whether SB01 drew on the Manila letters is not recorded

sources.record: Francisco de Sande, "Relation of the Filipinas Islands", Manila, 7 June 1576. B&R vol. 4 (Cleveland, 1903), pp. 21–97 (read pp. 53–65). Translated by Rachel King.
sources.form: Primary document, report to the Crown
sources.perspective: The incoming Spanish governor. He wants troops, so he has a reason to say the China trade is poor and the Chinese weak. In the passages used his informants are not named.

position.interests: Arguing for troops and against the China trade as it stood

sources.record: Antonio de Morga, *Sucesos de las islas Filipinas* (Mexico, 1609), trans. Henry E. J. Stanley, *The Philippine Islands, Moluccas, Siam, Cambodia, Japan, and China, at the Close of the Sixteenth Century* (Hakluyt Society, London, 1868), pp. 336, 340, 347.
sources.perspective: A judge (*oidor*) of the Manila Audiencia, writing for a European readership about 35 years after 1573. Context for the 1570s, not a witness.

position.role: Spanish judge of the Manila Audiencia

sources.record: José de Acosta, *Historia natural y moral de las Indias* (Seville, 1590). English: *The Natural and Moral History of the Indies*, from Edward Grimston's 1604 translation, ed. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society, London, 1880), vol. 1, Book 4, ch. 7, pp. 201–203.
sources.form: Primary treatise, in an early English translation (1604 spelling)
sources.perspective: Jesuit missionary and naturalist writing for a European readership. A different edition and language from Potosí's S02.

sources.record: William L. Schurz, "Mexico, Peru, and the Manila Galleon", *Hispanic American Historical Review* 1:4 (November 1918), 389–402.
sources.perspective: A US historian of Latin America, Spanish-centred. He cites archive letters that I did not open. Eight decades old. Use for what the cited letters say, not as the last word.

position.focus: The Manila galleon trade between Mexico, Peru and the Philippines, from Spanish archive letters.
position.note: Cites a Velasco letter in the archive (not free) and Bancroft (1883), which we do not hold.

sources.record: *Ming Shi-lu*, Wanli year 17, month 4, day 20 (2 June 1589), trans. Geoff Wade, *Southeast Asia in the Ming Shi-lu: an open access resource* (Singapore: Asia Research Institute and NUS Press).
sources.form: Primary document, court record, English translation by a named translator
sources.perspective: The Ming court's historians. The standpoint is imperial: security, licensing, tax. Merchants are subjects, not authors.

sources.record: Memorial to the Council by citizens of the Filipinas Islands, Santiago de Vera and others, Manila, [26 July] 1586 (the date is bracketed by the editors). B&R vol. 6 (Cleveland, 1903), pp. 157 ff. (used pp. 166–167). Translated by James A. Robertson, Emma Helen Blair and Robert W. Haight.
sources.perspective: Manila's citizens, who want the Chinese trade kept for themselves and the Mexican money kept out.

position.role: Citizens of Manila, with Santiago de Vera
position.interests: Keeping the Chinese trade for the citizens of Manila

sources.record: Alonso Fernández de Castro, *Principal points in regard to the trade of the Filipinas*, [1602?]. B&R vol. 12 (Cleveland, 1904), pp. 46 ff. (used pp. 50–51). Translated by Jose M. and Clara M. Asensio and Emma Helen Blair.
sources.perspective: A lawyer arguing for restrictions on Mexican and Peruvian trade. The date is B&R's guess.

position.audience: The crown, via a printed pamphlet
position.interests: Restricting the Mexican and Peruvian trade

sources.record: Gonzalo Ronquillo de Peñalosa to Felipe II, Manila, 16 June 1582. B&R vol. 5 (Cleveland, 1903), pp. 23 ff. (used p. 30). Translated by Jose M. and Clara M. Asensio.
sources.perspective: The governor reporting his own acts.

sources.record: Editors' footnote 75 (Emma Helen Blair and James A. Robertson) to the letter of Andrés de Mirandaola, B&R vol. 3 (Cleveland, 1903), p. 226. It quotes a letter of the Viceroy of New Spain dated 9 January 1574. The editors give no archive reference and the letter was not found in any free volume. Translator of the quoted passage: not named in the volume.
sources.form: Editors' note quoting a primary letter we have not read
sources.perspective: Modern editors (1903) passing on a viceroy's words. The same footnote adds hearsay ("I am told that they took away more than forty thousand ducats"); that figure is in no Claim.

position.proximity: Appeared in 1903; quotes a letter of January 1574
position.focus: The viceroy's report that the Chinese took gold and silver in payment.

sources.record: [Francisco de Sande], "Relation and description of the Phelipinas Islands", Manila, 8 June 1577. Blair & Robertson (eds.), *The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898*, vol. 4 (Cleveland, 1903), pp. 98-118 (read p. 101). From a manuscript in the Archivo de Indias, Sevilla. Translated by José M. Ascensio (name as printed in vol. 4's front matter). The editors print only the part that is new compared with Sande's 1576 report.
sources.form: Primary document, report to the Crown
sources.perspective: The governor of the Philippines, two years in office, writing to the king about money, gold and the state of the royal estate. He wants the colony funded and is arguing that his own management is sound.

position.interests: Showing he had put the royal estate in order while asking for support
position.note: same voice as SB03, so the two are not two witnesses

sources.record: Letter to Felipe II, Santiago de Vera and others, Manila, 26 June 1588. B&R vol. 7 (Cleveland, 1903), pp. 52-63 (read p. 57). From the original manuscript in the Archivo General de Indias, Sevilla. Translated by Jose M. and Clara M. Asensio (vol. 7 front matter: "the others, by Jose M. and Clara M. Asensio").
sources.perspective: The governor of the Philippines, reporting the fort he was building and how he paid for it.

position.interests: Reporting and justifying his fort and the taxes that paid for it
position.note: Vera also signed the 1586 memorial (SB08, ML7); a different document and year, but the same man. Count with care.

sources.record: Dennis O. Flynn and Arturo Giráldez, "Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571", *Journal of World History* 6:2 (Fall 1995), 201–221.
sources.perspective: Two economic historians arguing a thesis: world trade began in 1571 and China's demand for silver drove it. They write against a Europe-centred account. Their Pacific figures come from other scholars (Chuan, TePaske, Barrett), not from their own archive work.

position.focus: The world silver market from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century, with China as the main buyer.
position.note: On p. 204 they say Chuan built his Manila estimate from Blair and Robertson, the collection our SB01 to SB13 come from. Two of their page references do not match their own reference list (Chuan 1969, p. 79; "TePaske 1981").

sources.record: Dennis O. Flynn and Arturo Giráldez, "Path dependence, time lags and the birth of globalisation: A critique of O'Rourke and Williamson", *European Review of Economic History* 8:1 (April 2004), 81–108.
sources.perspective: The same two authors answering O'Rourke and Williamson by name. They restate the 1571 thesis and add ecology and population to the case. They quote their opponents' 2002 articles at length.

position.focus: When globalisation began, argued against the price-convergence test.
position.note: Same authors and same thesis as SB14; not a second witness.

sources.record: Kevin H. O'Rourke and Jeffrey G. Williamson, "Once more: When did globalisation begin?", *European Review of Economic History* 8:1 (April 2004), 109–117.
sources.perspective: Two economists who define globalisation as market integration and test it with prices. They say their work does not deal with silver flows and that they lack Asian price evidence.

position.focus: Whether trade between continents before 1800 integrated markets, measured by commodity prices.
position.note: A nine-page restatement. The evidence is in their two 2002 articles, which we have not read.

sources.record: William S. Atwell, "International Bullion Flows and the Chinese Economy circa 1530–1650", *Past & Present* 95 (May 1982), 68–90.
sources.perspective: A historian of Ming China. He reads the silver trade for what it did to China's economy and to the dynasty. His Manila material comes from Schurz (1939), Ch'üan Han-sheng, Blair and Robertson, and Morga.

position.focus: Japanese and Spanish-American silver entering Ming China, and its effects there.
position.note: His 1573 cargo sentence (p. 73) comes through Schurz and matches the list in SB02; it is not an independent witness. His ratio table (p. 82) is from P'eng Hsin-wei.

sources.record: Jan de Vries, "The limits of globalization in the early modern world", *Economic History Review* 63:3 (August 2010), 710–733.
sources.perspective: An economic historian of Europe. He tests the globalisation claims against his own figures for the Cape route between Europe and Asia. The Pacific route is outside his data.

position.focus: How much Europe-Asia trade by sea grew from 1501 to 1795, and why it stayed limited.
position.note: Disagrees with both sides in part: "soft" globalisation yes, "hard" no.

sources.record: Richard von Glahn, *Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000–1700* (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1996), ch. 4, "Foreign Silver and China's 'Silver Century', 1550–1650", pp. 113–141.
sources.perspective: A historian of Chinese money, reading the silver trade from the Chinese side. His Manila figures come from Chaunu's customs series and TePaske; his Japan figures from Souza and Innes. He sets his own estimates below the ones most often quoted.

position.focus: How foreign silver reached Ming China from 1550 to 1650, by which routes and in what amounts.
position.note: The chapter's endnotes are not in our file. Its Manila series start in 1577 (ships) and 1586 (customs); it has no figure for 1573.

sources.record: Richard von Glahn, *Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000–1700* (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1996), ch. 3, "Coinage in the Dawning Age of Silver, 1435–1570", pp. 83–112 (read pp. 83, 97, 112).
sources.perspective: The same historian on China before Manila existed: how silver took over taxes and large payments while coin decayed. The chapter does not mention Manila.

position.focus: Ming coin and uncoined silver from 1435 to 1570.
position.note: The chapter's endnotes are not in our file, so its sources are not checked.
